newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: French bond futures followed Bunds higher in a calm session with calls for lower rates from within the Bank of France's inner sanctum buoying sentiment despite a jittery franc.

A bond trader at a French bank said without any extra drive from the United States, where markets were closed for a holiday, the futures contract stalled at a new contract high of 128.30 as it "ran out of fuel".
Conflicting forces at the short end of the curve left March PIBOR higher on the day. Traders said domestic investors were selling PIBOR contracts while non-residents were buyers.
They said the reverse was the case for the franc with domestic investors buying the French currency at the lows after widespread non-resident selling.

The franc fell to a low of 3.3972 against the mark after Bank of France monetary policy council member Jean-Pierre Gerard said in a newspaper interview German lack of understanding on monetary and exchange rate policy may make a change in the mark-franc parity necessary.
He also called for a rise in the dollar/franc rate to 6.00. The dollar rallied to a high of 5.2105 against the franc from a low of 5.1715 and was at 5.20 at 1650 GMT.
One economist said the latest round of statements might be part of an orchestrated campaign to put pressure on the Germans to lower interest rates, and thus push up the dollar.

"They are not all loose cannons. I rather think that it may be (President Jacques) Chirac behind this, putting pressure on Germany, saying it is going to be very difficult here to continue on the road to monetary union," he said.

Jean-Francois Mercier, economist at Salomon Brothers, said in a note while the comments from French officials highlighted differences with Germany, the authorities would be unlikely to force a change in policy given their commitment to EMU.

"Most likely French public statements of EMU-related concerns represent an attempt to persuade German policymakers to accept a less stringent version of the stability pact, rather than a serious desire to weaken the franc-mark parity," he said.

A foreign exchange trader in Paris said even though the dissenting voices at the Bank of France were in a minority "non-residents have been astonished by the lack of order and are beginning ask themselves questions about the timing of EMU."
However, a PIBOR trader said non-residents were also betting the eventual outcome of the debate would be lower French interest rates and were buyers of PIBOR futures.

Traders said one reason for the heightened expectation of lower rates was that two of the policy council members deemed "hawks" by French newspaper Liberation have their mandates up for renewal at the end of the year, fueling speculation they will be replaced by advocates of a looser monetary policy.
"The doves are showing their colours and increasing the pressure," said the PIBOR trader.
"Market perceptions that the replacement of two MPC members by year-end could -- in theory -- alter the council's majority may add to near-term risks for the franc," Mercier said.

Those who watch the Bank of France closely said that doves were still in the minority in calling for faster rate cuts. On Thursday the Bank announced it was holding the intervention rate unchanged at 3.20 percent after its regular council meeting.

There was little reaction to a 0.9 percent rise in third quarter French GDP as it was in line with expectations and did nothing to change the overall picture of a sluggish economy and an almost certain fourth quarter slowdown.
